prize_parts.citation: for the observation of a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with the IceCube observatory, opening neutrino astronomy

statement.case_for: I keep B061 as my preferred configuration after reading the whole first round. The 2013 observation of a diffuse TeV-PeV neutrino flux in a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice is a discovery made in nature: a new messenger that carries information from the cosmic-ray accelerators that no photon or charged particle can give us. It has stood for more than a decade, has been reproduced in several channels (through-going muons, cascades, starting events), and now has two partial source results, TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic plane, which show that the window is already delivering astrophysics and not only a count rate. Putting the discovery first, as this committee should, the question is whether the IceCube observation changed what we know about the universe, and it did. I also take the lattice-clock case seriously: it is the best-attributed and best-reproduced candidate on the shortlist and I would accept it as a prize. The reason I do not move is that, after the round-1 answers to my question about what the clock has revealed, the realised physics is millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and bounds on drifting constants, which are very fine results on a known effect, while the neutrino flux is a first look at a population of sources nobody had seen.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the weakest point and I will not pretend otherwise. IceCube is a collaboration of hundreds that descends from DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA, we may credit at most three people, and Halzen, Karle and Spiering stand for leadership of the concept, construction and analysis rather than for a single decisive act, so the allocation has an element of judgement. The origin of most of the diffuse flux is still unidentified, so a sceptic can say we are rewarding the opening of a field before it has delivered its first firm answer. Only three members ranked B061 at opening and one preferred configuration names it, so even if I am right on science I may be asking the committee to carry an award that it cannot defend as cleanly as a two-name award for B010. I also concede that a strict reading of the criterion that a discovery must be clearly groundbreaking and well attributed favours B010 on the second half of that sentence.

responses.point: Lindroth asks whether the TXS 0506+056 and Galactic-plane results are strong enough to say the cosmic-ray origin question has been answered, or only that a flux exists, and asks which of the three was decisive.
responses.response: Fair question, and the honest answer is that the origin question is not answered; it has been opened. TXS 0506+056 is a single blazar at about the three-sigma level in the archival data, and the Galactic plane is a diffuse correlation, so neither identifies the dominant sources of the isotropic flux. My claim is narrower: the detection of the flux itself, which no earlier instrument could make, is the discovery, in the same way that the first gravitational-wave detection was recognised before source populations were mapped. On attribution, I would ask the expert reports to separate the people who made the 2013 diffuse-flux observation possible, Halzen as the driver of the concept and of AMANDA-to-IceCube, Karle through detector construction and calibration, Spiering through the analysis lineage, and I accept that the committee may judge that distinction too fine.

responses.point: Johansson says a clock is an instrument-based discovery in my own sense, since it measures something nature does (time dilation), that the three-name IceCube credit is harder to defend than a documented pair, and that he would not stand in the way of B061.
responses.response: I accept the point that a clock is not merely a gadget, and I would not call B010 an engineering prize. The difference I still draw is between measuring a known effect more precisely and seeing something nobody had seen: gravitational redshift over a millimetre confirms general relativity, while a diffuse neutrino flux of unknown origin is a surprise. I accept your attribution argument in full as the strongest reason to prefer B010, and I thank you for not blocking B061; I would rather have my reservation tested by the expert reports than win by default.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice-clock agreement is earned, with independent clocks at NIST, PTB, SYRTE and RIKEN agreeing at about 1e-18, with a clean Katori-Ye attribution and with relativistic time dilation resolved over millimetres and bounds on drifting constants already in hand.
responses.response: That answers the question I put to you in round 1, and I am grateful for the specifics. I accept that the reproducibility is superb and that the maturity is not in doubt. I would still ask that the citation be worded around the magic-wavelength lattice and the 1e-18 regime, and not around time and frequency in general, because I share your own concern that without this the prize reads as a successor to the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. I do not think the SI redefinition should count for or against the timing, and I would keep it out of the scientific case.

responses.point: Olsson says she ranked IceCube fifth, that the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND lineage and thin source identification weaken the credit, and that a few more years would strengthen the case, but she would not oppose it.
responses.response: I accept the lineage point: the intellectual history of DUMAND and Baikal is real and the committee should say in the citation what exactly is being credited. I do not accept that waiting for source identification is the right test, because the discovery of the flux was made in 2013 and the credited people are in their later years, so delay has a cost for the fairness of the award as well as for its freshness. I agree with you that the question is not whether the flux is real but whether three names can carry it, which is exactly where the reports must be sharp.

responses.point: Pearce moved to B010 as his preferred choice, keeps B061 as his first alternative, and says that attribution among Halzen, Karle and Spiering is less clean than I suggested and that he cannot call B061 the consensus choice today.
responses.response: I agree that I cannot call it the consensus and I do not claim to. I also note, with respect, that you have a field proximity to B061 and that you correctly refused to let affinity decide, so your move to B010 does not weaken the science of B061 in my eyes. I would ask that your alternative stay on record for the final ballot: if the reports show a decisive contribution within the three names, there may be more support for B061 than a first-round count suggests.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from B051 to B010 after the opening ballots, accepting that the lattice clock is a measurement-capability prize more than a discovery of a new phenomenon, with theory explaining the systematic shifts, and says that if the committee wants a discovery in nature B051 is the better case.
responses.response: I note that you grant the same distinction that I draw, a capability against a phenomenon, and I take your point that the agreement between calculation and measurement is a real strength of B010. I would resist the idea that B051 is the stronger discovery case at present: you yourself list the pairing mechanism and the omission of Cao and Fatemi as open, and a prize that leaves out the lead experimental authors would be harder to defend than the IceCube trio.

uncertainties: Whether the expert reports identify a decisive contribution to the 2013 diffuse-flux observation among Halzen, Karle and Spiering, or point to credited names outside the three.
Whether independent neutrino telescopes (ANTARES, Baikal-GVD, KM3NeT) confirm the diffuse flux strongly enough to close the maturity question.
Whether the committee, with five of eight members now on B010, will in the final ballot weigh a discovery in nature above a clean two-name measurement prize.
Whether B010 can be worded to remain clearly distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which would change how strongly I regard it as an alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No apparent conflict on B061: my supervisor David Gross, my mentor Hector Rubinstein and my co-author Thomas Van Riet are not among the credited names. As in round 1, I cannot verify from my profile whether Uppsala has an institutional role in neutrino astronomy, and I would recuse myself from B061 if the committee finds one. No conflict on B010 or B047 is known to me.
